reason: The text demonstrates that strict hierarchy is fundamentally important and extensively reinforced throughout. Multiple hierarchical structures are clearly established: divine hierarchy (God > angel > people), familial authority (parents have recognized status, though sometimes tested), political/military hierarchy (Philistine sarnim as rulers, Israel subjugated under Philistine dominion), and tribal organization (Judah's three thousand men under implicit leadership). The Nazirite vow itself constitutes a sacred hierarchical obligation from birth. While Samson acts independently in specific instances (insisting on the Philistine woman despite parental objection, being vulnerable to Delilah's manipulation), these are portrayed as personal failings or consequences of human weakness rather than endorsements of rejecting hierarchy. The overarching narrative structure—conflict between nations, divine calling, family obligation—all depend upon hierarchical frameworks being maintained and binding.
